content: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels are regulated through a negative feedback mechanism. Estrogens play a role in reducing the elevated levels of gonadotropins that are typically observed in postmenopausal women. Structure There is limited information available regarding the structural composition of conjugated estrogens in the drug label. Pharmacodynamics The pharmacodynamic properties of conjugated estrogens are not extensively detailed in the drug label. Pharmacokinetics Conjugated estrogens are water-soluble and are efficiently absorbed through the skin, mucous membranes, and gastrointestinal tract after being released from the drug formulation. The distribution of exogenous estrogens in the body is similar to that of endogenous estrogens. Estrogens are widely distributed throughout the body, with higher concentrations found in sex hormone target organs. In the bloodstream, estrogens primarily circulate bound to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) and albumin. Exogenous estrogens undergo metabolism in a manner similar to endogenous estrogens. Circulating estrogens exist in a dynamic equilibrium of metabolic interconversions, primarily occurring in the liver. Estradiol is reversibly converted to estrone, and both can be further metabolized into estriol, which is a major urinary metabolite. Estrogens also undergo enterohepatic recirculation. This process involves sulfate and glucuronide conjugation in the liver, biliary secretion of these conjugates into the intestine, hydrolysis in the intestine, and subsequent reabsorption. In postmenopausal women, a significant proportion of circulating estrogens exist as sulfate conjugates, particularly estrone sulfate, which serves as a circulating reservoir for the formation of more active estrogens. Estradiol, estrone, and estriol are excreted in the urine, along with their glucuronide and sulfate conjugates. No pharmacokinetic studies have been conducted in special populations, such as patients with renal or hepatic impairment. Data from a single-dose drug-drug interaction study involving oral conjugated estrogens (CE) and medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA) indicate that the pharmacokinetic profiles of both drugs remain unaltered when coadministered. No other clinical drug-drug interaction studies have been conducted with conjugated estrogens. Both in vitro and in vivo studies have demonstrated that estrogens are partially metabolized by the cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) enzyme. Consequently, inducers or inhibitors of CYP3A4 may influence the metabolism of estrogen drugs. CYP3A4 inducers, such as St. John’s wort (Hypericum perforatum), phenobarbital, carbamazepine, and rifampin, may reduce plasma concentrations of estrogens, potentially leading to decreased therapeutic effects and/or alterations in uterine bleeding patterns. Conversely, CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as erythromycin, clarithromycin, ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, and grapefruit juice, may increase plasma concentrations of estrogens, potentially resulting in an increased risk of side effects. Nonclinical Toxicology There is limited information available regarding the nonclinical toxicology of conjugated estrogens in the drug label. Clinical Studies The Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) study evaluated the effects of conjugated estrogens (0.625 mg) alone or in combination with medroxyprogesterone acetate (2.5 mg) compared to placebo in the prevention of certain chronic diseases. The primary endpoint of the study was the incidence of coronary heart disease (CHD), with invasive breast cancer serving as the primary adverse outcome. A global index was used to assess the earliest occurrence of CHD, invasive breast cancer, stroke, pulmonary embolism (PE), endometrial cancer (only in the CE plus MPA substudy), colorectal cancer, hip fracture, or death from other causes. These studies did not evaluate the effects of CE alone or CE plus MPA on menopausal symptoms. WHI Estrogen-Alone Substudy The WHI estrogen-alone substudy was terminated prematurely due to an observed increased risk of stroke. It was determined that no further information could be obtained regarding the risks and benefits of estrogen-alone therapy for the predetermined primary endpoints. Data from the study, which lasted an average of 6.8 years, are presented in the findings.
